newsitem.title: USA: Jury hears about Trade Center bomb victims.
newsitem.headline: Jury hears about Trade Center bomb victims.

text.p: Jurors in the trial of accused World Trade Centre bombing mastermind Ramzi Yousef on Thursday looked at grisly photographs of the six people killed in the 1993 explosion.
Some jurors wept and shuddered at the sight of the disfigured corpses and the testimony about their violent deaths from a medical examiner, Dr. Jacqueline Lee.
Of the two Moslem militants on trial in federal court, Yousef was accused of building and planting the bomb.
His alleged accomplice Eyad Ismoil was accused of driving the van that carried the powerful device into the World Trade Center's underground garage on Feb. 26, 1993.
The blast at Manhattan's famed 110-story twin towers killed six people, injured more than 1,000 and caused more than $550 million in damage.
Prosecutors say the two men were part of a war of terrorism against the United States and wanted to kill thousands of people to retaliate for U.S. support for Israel.

Defence attorney Louis Aidala, who represents Ismoil, tried unsuccessfully to prevent prosecutors from allowing Lee to present graphic details about the victims' deaths. He also argued before U.S. District Judge Kevin Duffy that the photos would inflame and prejudice the jury.
One of the victims was Monica Smith, a pregnant secretary, and the intensity of the blast stamped the patterned imprint of her sweater into her shoulder, the medical examiner said.

At an earlier trial in the bombing case, jurors saw a picture of Smith's exposed abdomen and were told about the damage done to her foetus. Four other Moslem fundamentalists were convicted on charges stemming from the bombing in 1994.
As the jury looked at these photographs, Yousef stared straight ahead and Ismoil kept his head down.

The other bombing victims were Wilfredo Mercado, a restaurant worker; Steven Knapp, a maintenance supervisor; William Macko, a maintenance worker; Robert Kirkpatrick, a locksmith, and John DiGiovanni, a dental salesman.
Mercado's body was buried under tons of rubble and was not found until two weeks after the explosion.
Lee testified the victims died of blunt impact trauma.
Testimony was scheduled to resume on Monday morning with an agent of the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service, who is expected to testify that Yousef entered the United States in 1992.

Ismoil's mother, Najlah Ismail, who spells her name differently than her son, attended court on Thursday for the first time since her son went on trial. She is the first relative to attend any of the bombing trials.
Speaking with reporters through an interpreter during a break, she said she would have preferred her son be tried alone and not with his co-defendant.
"She is so sure Eyad has nothing to do with this and that is why she would like him to be tried alone," the interpretor said.
Yousef and Ismoil fled the country the night of the explosion. Yousef was captured in Pakistan in 1995 and Ismoil was arrested in Jordan last year.

In a statement Ismoil gave authorities after his arrest, he said he was an unsuspecting dupe and thought he was delivering boxes of soap for Yousef, who told him that he was setting up a soap and shampoo company.
Ismoil's mother arrived in New York on Wednesday from the Jordanian village of Jarash.
"I'm not just saying this as his mother but he loves America," she said.
